title: Acid-base equilibria: Kz, Kb, Kw and buffers - 123 school
heading: Acid-base equilibria: Kz, Kb, Kw and buffers
intro: Test your knowledge by typing your answer and comparing it with the correct answer. Then click 'Check answers'.

questions.q: Give the equilibrium condition of a weak acid HZ in water: HZ + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + Z<sup>–</sup>
questions.a: K<sub>z</sub> = [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] · [Z<sup>–</sup>] / [HZ]

questions.q: Give the equilibrium condition of NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>–</sup>
questions.a: K<sub>b</sub> = [NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>] · [OH<sup>–</sup>] / [NH<sub>3</sub>]

questions.q: Why is H<sub>2</sub>O not in the fraction of K<sub>z</sub> and K<sub>b</sub>?
questions.a: Water is the solvent and its concentration is practically constant. It is already included in the constant

questions.q: Give the equilibrium condition for the self-ionisation equilibrium of water: 2 H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>–</sup>
questions.a: K<sub>w</sub> = [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] · [OH<sup>–</sup>]

questions.q: What is the value of K<sub>w</sub> at 298 K?
What relationship exists between pH and pOH at 298 K?
questions.a: pH + pOH = 14.00

questions.q: What relationship exists between K<sub>z</sub> of an acid, K<sub>b</sub> of the conjugate base and K<sub>w</sub>?
questions.a: K<sub>z</sub> · K<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>w</sub>

questions.q: The acid HZ has K<sub>z</sub> = 1.0·10<sup>–5</sup>. Calculate K<sub>b</sub> of Z<sup>–</sup>
questions.a: K<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>w</sub> / K<sub>z</sub> = 1.0·10<sup>–14</sup> / 1.0·10<sup>–5</sup> = 1.0·10<sup>–9</sup>

questions.q: What does a larger K<sub>z</sub> say about an acid?
questions.a: The acid is stronger: relatively more H<sup>+</sup> is donated to water

questions.q: What is the difference between a strong and a weak acid in water?
questions.a: A strong acid reacts (almost) completely with water. A weak acid reacts only partly, an equilibrium forms

questions.q: Calculate the pH of 0.10 mol/L HCl
questions.a: HCl is a strong acid, so [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = 0.10 mol/L and pH = 1.00

questions.q: Calculate the pH of 0.010 mol/L NaOH
questions.a: NaOH is a strong base, so [OH<sup>–</sup>] = 0.010 mol/L, pOH = 2.00 and pH = 12.00

questions.q: Which approximation do you use to calculate the pH of a weak acid?
questions.a: [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = [Z<sup>–</sup>] and [HZ] is practically equal to the initial concentration. Then [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = K<sub>z</sub> · [HZ]

questions.q: Calculate the pH of 0.10 mol/L of a weak acid with K<sub>z</sub> = 1.0·10<sup>–5</sup>
Calculate the pH of 0.10 mol/L acetic acid. Take K<sub>z</sub> = 1.7·10<sup>–5</sup>
A solution has pH = 3.00. What is [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>]?
questions.a: [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>–pH</sup> = 1.0·10<sup>–3</sup> mol/L

questions.q: Calculate the pH of 0.10 mol/L of a weak base with K<sub>b</sub> = 1.0·10<sup>–5</sup>
You dilute a solution of a weak acid 100 times. How does the pH change approximately?
questions.a: [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] becomes 10 times smaller (square root of 100), so the pH becomes about 1 higher

questions.q: You dilute a solution of a strong acid 100 times. How does the pH change?
questions.a: [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] becomes 100 times smaller, so the pH becomes 2 higher

questions.q: What is a buffer?
questions.a: A solution whose pH hardly changes when you add a little acid or base

questions.q: What does a buffer consist of?
questions.a: A weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) in comparable amounts

questions.q: How does an acetic acid / acetate buffer work when you add a little acid?
questions.a: The added H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> reacts with the base CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>–</sup>. So the pH stays almost the same

questions.q: How does an acetic acid / acetate buffer work when you add a little base?
questions.a: The added OH<sup>–</sup> reacts with the acid CH<sub>3</sub>COOH. So the pH stays almost the same

questions.q: Why is a mixture of HCl and NaCl not a buffer?
questions.a: HCl is a strong acid and Cl<sup>–</sup> is not a base that can bind H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>. So there is no weak acid-base pair

questions.q: Give an example of a buffer in the body
questions.a: The H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> / HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> system in the blood (pH about 7.4)

questions.q: What is the conjugate base of acetic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH)?
questions.a: CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>–</sup> (acetate ion)

questions.q: A buffer contains as much acid HZ as base Z<sup>–</sup>. The acid has K<sub>z</sub> = 1.0·10<sup>–5</sup>. What is the pH?
questions.a: K<sub>z</sub> = [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] · [Z<sup>–</sup>] / [HZ] and [Z<sup>–</sup>] = [HZ], so [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = K<sub>z</sub> = 1.0·10<sup>–5</sup> mol/L and pH = 5.00

questions.q: When does a buffer stop working?
questions.a: When so much acid or base has been added that one of the two components of the buffer is used up

questions.q: Acetic acid (K<sub>z</sub> = 1.7·10<sup>–5</sup>) reacts with ammonia (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> has K<sub>z</sub> = 5.6·10<sup>–10</sup>). Does this equilibrium lie to the left or to the right?
questions.a: K = K<sub>z</sub>(acetic acid) / K<sub>z</sub>(NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) = 1.7·10<sup>–5</sup> / 5.6·10<sup>–10</sup> = 3.0·10<sup>4</sup>. K is large, so the equilibrium lies far to the right

questions.q: What is the pH at the equivalence point when you titrate acetic acid with NaOH: lower than, equal to or higher than 7?
questions.a: Higher than 7, because CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>–</sup> is a weak base
